options: The price an investor pays to buy the bond
The stated annual interest rate paid on the bond's face value
The date the bond matures and is repaid
The market's current risk-free rate
questions.explain: The coupon rate is the stated annual interest rate, expressed as a percentage of face value, that the issuer pays to bondholders.

questions.q: If a bond's market price falls, what happens to its yield to maturity, all else equal?
options: The yield to maturity falls as well
The yield to maturity rises
The yield to maturity is unaffected by price changes
The yield to maturity becomes negative automatically
questions.explain: Yield to maturity and price move inversely: as price falls, the same future coupons and face value represent a higher percentage return, so yield rises.

questions.q: What does the "term structure of interest rates" (yield curve) show?
options: The historical price of a single bond over time
The yield of comparable bonds plotted against their time to maturity
The default probability of every bond issuer in a market
The dividend yield of equities compared to bond yields
questions.explain: The term structure plots yield against maturity for otherwise-comparable bonds, showing how the rate for lending changes with how long the money is locked up.

questions.q: What does an inverted yield curve typically suggest?
options: The economy is accelerating with no risks ahead
Short-term yields exceed long-term yields, which has historically often preceded economic slowdowns
Bond prices and yields have stopped being inversely related
The central bank has eliminated all short-term interest rates
questions.explain: An inverted curve means short maturities yield more than long ones, an unusual pattern historically associated with markets expecting future rate cuts and economic slowdowns.

questions.q: Why are US Treasury yields used as the market's "risk-free rate"?
options: Because Treasuries pay the highest yield of any bond
Because Treasuries are backed by the US government, considered to have effectively zero default risk in its own currency
Because Treasuries are the only bonds with a yield curve
Because Treasuries have no maturity date
questions.explain: US Treasuries carry essentially no default risk, so their yields serve as the baseline risk-free rate against which other investments' risk premiums are measured.
